paras: It is often said that critics agree about the great productions and only argue about the mediocre ones, and the current revival is a useful test of that claim, because it has been reviewed twice by the same newspaper and the two verdicts barely touch. The first, written after the opening night, called the staging atmospheric and the lead performance understated to the point of invisibility. The second, published three weeks later, described the same performance as the most gripping thing on a London stage this year. Nothing on stage had been changed. What had changed was the audience.

This is less mysterious than it sounds. A production that is built as a slow burn is punished by an opening night, where an audience of critics and investors is looking for an effect in the first ten minutes and is unusually resistant to being made to wait. Three weeks later the theatre is full of people who paid, who have heard something about the play, and who arrive prepared to give it time. The performance was not improved; it was finally being watched by the audience it had been designed for. It is now widely believed in the industry that opening-night reviews measure the room as much as the work, and several papers have quietly moved their reviewers to the second week.

None of which means that reviews are worthless, and the temptation to conclude that is the lazy one. A review that says a production is uneven, and then says exactly which twenty minutes fall flat, is worth more than any number of stars. The problem is not judgement. It is the verdict without the reasons, which is what a rating is: a play can be panned and still be worth your evening, and a play that is thought to be a masterpiece can be, on the night you go, overrated and far too long. The useful question is never whether the critic liked it. It is what the critic was looking at.

Opening-night audiences are more knowledgeable than audiences three weeks later.

items: It is often said that critics only argue about the mediocre productions.
The staging was described as atmospheric by almost everybody.

Nothing had been changed. What had changed was the audience.

listenings.text: I stopped giving stars about four years ago and my editor has never quite forgiven me. The argument for stars is that readers are busy, which is true. The argument against them is that a star rating is a verdict with the reasons removed, and the reasons are the only part of my job that has any value. If I tell you a production is uneven, you have learned almost nothing. If I tell you that the first act is twenty minutes too long and that the second is the best thing the company has done in a decade, you can decide for yourself whether that trade is worth your Saturday. The other thing I have learned, slowly and against my instincts, is that I should not review anything on the opening night. The room is full of people who are not there to watch a play. They are there to be seen having watched it, and that changes what happens on stage more than anybody admits.

I saw the same play twice, ten years apart, with two different casts, and I have thought about it ever since, because I did not change my mind about the production. I changed my mind about the ending. The first time I was thirty and I thought the ending was sentimental and unearned, and I remember being quite pleased with myself for noticing. The second time I was forty and the same ending completely destroyed me. Nothing in the staging was different. What was different is that I had been through the thing the play is about, and at thirty I simply had not. I am not sure what that says about criticism, honestly. Maybe only that a review is a record of what one person could see on one evening, which is worth reading and is not the same thing as a measurement.
